newsitem.title: POLAND: Tight Polish money market seen buoying zloty.
newsitem.headline: Tight Polish money market seen buoying zloty.

text.p: Polish money markets are expected to remain tight this week, limiting demand for T-bills at Monday's primary auction and keeping upward pressure on the zloty, analysts said.

"Liquidity is not likely to increase this week, and (money) market rates will remain high as cash outflows, mainly caused by fast growing credit, shortened bank positions from the start of the month," said Aleksandra Watroba of Bank Slaski SA.
One-day deposit rates jumped some five percentage points last week to close near the 25-percent Lombard rate, while one-month deposits rose more than six points to 24.8 on Friday.
Some analysts said the market would remain cash-strapped for the entire month, while others said that the squeeze could start easing by the end of next week.

"If cash appears at the end of next week, on December 20, it could signal that banks have long reserve positions and want to place surpluses and that rates will be lower for the rest of the month," one senior dealer at a Polish bank said.
However, analysts said there was little hope of one-day deposit rates falling to the main central bank drainage rate of 19.16 percent this week.
Analysts said the short money market would likely severely curb bids at Monday's 1.1 billion zloty primary auction, which could drive up yields if the treasury allows prices to drop.

"Nobody wants to invest in T-bills at primary auctions now because yields on the secondary market are much higher as banks sell their papers to improve liquidity," said Wojciech Labryga, T-bill dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
Analysts said banks may bid for the benchmark 52-week T-bill at around 19.65 percent, up from an average yield of 19.56 percent at last week's auction.
They said foreigners may try to enter large amounts at high yields to tempt the ministry into cutting minimum prices but said the corporate sector would not bid at the tender.
"Corporates can get more attractive offers from banks than from the finance ministry so, they are not likely to bid much at Monday's tender," one foreign dealer here said.
Analysts expected banks to bid for the 26-week T-bill at five to 15 points above last week's 19.25 percent and for perhaps even more for the 13-week paper, which last yielded 18.77 percent.
They said the zloty would likely stay underpinned around 2.6 percent from the trading band centre, or the parity rate, this week as the money market remained strapped for cash.

The zloty, which closed last week at a six-month high of 2.74 percent from the parity rate, was expected to feel further upward pressure because some foreign banks in Poland were expected to increase their capital before the end of the year.
Analysts estimated some $100 million from capital increases could go through the forex market before 1997.
